lessons.title: Offside: the blue line rule
lessons.objective: State what makes an entry offside.

payload.prompt: If both skates cross the blue line before the puck fully crosses, it is offside. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker with both skates over the blue line as the puck remains in the neutral zone.

explanation.correct: Correct. That is the offside rule: both skates over the leading edge before the puck fully crosses.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is when both skates completely cross the blue line before the puck does. This is the definition.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both skates over the line before the puck, that's offside.

payload.prompt: One skate touching the blue line keeps you onside. True or false?

scene.alt: A skater with one blade on the blue line as the puck approaches.

explanation.correct: True. A skate on the line is onside. You must be completely over (both skates past the line) to be offside.
explanation.incorrect: If one skate touches the line, you are onside. Only both skates fully crossing the line makes you offside.
explanation.sayThisLine: Skate on the line is fine, both skates over is offside.

payload.prompt: Soccer also has offside. Is the hockey rule the same?

options.text: Yes, exactly the same rule
No. Hockey is about the blue line and skates; soccer is about the last defender and involvement.
Yes, both are about the last defender

explanation.correct: Right. Hockey offside is mechanical: it's the blue line, the puck and both skates. Soccer offside is about the last defender and involvement in the play. The shared word fools a lot of people.
explanation.incorrect: They only share a name. In hockey it's about the blue line, the puck and both skates; in soccer it's about the last defender and being involved in the play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hockey offside is the blue line, not like soccer at all.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to its role in offside.

pairs.definition: The boundary of the offensive zone; both skates crossing it before the puck means offside.
The edge of the blue line closer to the attacking zone where the offside judgment is made.
The offside rule requires both to cross completely for the violation to occur.

explanation.summary: Offside stops goal-hanging: the puck has to enter the zone first, or at least not behind a skater who is already all the way in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Offside is about the blue line and when your skates cross it.

payload.prompt: Can a player be offside in the neutral zone?

options.text: Yes, if they are ahead of the puck
No, offside only applies at the blue line into the offensive zone
Only if they are past center ice

explanation.correct: Right. Offside is called when entering the offensive zone at the blue line. The neutral zone has no offside rule.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is a zone-entry rule. The neutral zone is free; you go offside when entering the offensive zone early.

lessons.title: Be the linesman: offside
lessons.objective: Call offside plays correctly at real speed.

payload.prompt: When does the linesman blow the whistle for offside?

options.text: After the offside player touches the puck
Right away, once the puck crosses the line with a player already offside
Only if the offside player tries to score

explanation.correct: Right. The violation happens at the blue line, so the linesman whistles it then. The one exception is delayed offside, where play continues while the defense can bring the puck out.
explanation.incorrect: The call doesn't wait for a touch or a shot. It's made at the blue line, the moment the puck enters with a player already offside. (Delayed offside is the one exception.)
explanation.sayThisLine: It's dead at the blue line, no touch needed.

payload.prompt: Linesmen stand on the side of the ice to get the best angle on whether skates are over the line. True or false?

scene.alt: A linesman positioned on the side of the ice, looking perpendicular to the blue line.

explanation.correct: True. Linesmen skate along the boards near the blue line so they look straight across it, which is the clearest view of skates and puck.
explanation.incorrect: Linesmen work along the boards beside the blue line. From there they look straight across it to see whether skates or puck are over.

payload.prompt: Match the role to who does it.

pairs.definition: One of two officials stationed on the sides who watch for offside and icing.
When an attacker enters the offensive zone before the puck with both skates over the blue line.
Linesman's raised arm: delayed offside, play continues until the zone is cleared or the puck is touched.

explanation.summary: Linesmen call offside and icing; referees handle penalties. No flags in hockey: it's a whistle, or an arm for a delay.
explanation.sayThisLine: The linesman calls offside, not the ref.

payload.prompt: A common offside mistake: thinking that involvement in play matters. Does it?

options.text: Yes, if you don't touch it, you are not offside
No. Offside is about positioning when entering the zone, not involvement.
Only if the ref saw it

explanation.correct: Right. Offside is about where skates and puck are at the blue line. Whether the player touches the puck or helps the play doesn't matter; that's the soccer habit talking.
explanation.incorrect: Hockey offside is decided by skates and puck at the blue line, not by who touches what afterward. A player can be offside without ever touching the puck.

lessons.title: Delayed offside and tagging up
lessons.objective: Explain why play sometimes continues after an early entry.

payload.prompt: Order a delayed offside from entry to restart.

items.text: An attacker is over the blue line early as the puck enters
The linesman raises an arm and lets play continue
The defense gains control of the puck
Every attacker skates back and touches the blue line

explanation.correct: That's the flow. The early entry is noted with a raised arm, play continues while the defense has the puck, and the delay ends once the attackers tag up at the blue line.
explanation.incorrect: The early entry comes first, then the raised arm. The defense gets the puck, and only after all attackers tag up at the blue line does the offside disappear.
explanation.sayThisLine: Arm's up, just tag up and it's fine.

payload.prompt: If an offside attacker waits while the defense has the puck, the linesman blows the whistle immediately. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker waits in the zone while a defender has possession.

explanation.correct: False. With the defense in control, the linesman raises an arm and waits (delayed offside). If the puck leaves the zone or everyone tags up, no whistle.
explanation.incorrect: Not right away. A delayed offside means the linesman holds the whistle while the defense controls the puck and lets the attackers tag up.

payload.prompt: Match the term to what it means in delayed offside.

pairs.definition: Offside attackers skate back out and touch the blue line, cancelling the offside.
The defense gets the puck out of the zone, which also wipes out the delayed offside.
If the attacking team plays the puck while an attacker is still offside, the whistle blows.

explanation.summary: A delayed offside ends three ways: the attackers tag up, the defense clears the puck, or the attackers play it and the whistle blows.
explanation.sayThisLine: They all tagged up, so play on.

payload.prompt: If the attacking team touches the puck while someone is still offside, what happens?

options.text: Delayed offside ends and play continues normally
The linesman immediately calls offside
Only if the offside player touched it

explanation.correct: Right. The delay only protects the attackers while the defense has the puck. If the attacking team plays it and someone hasn't tagged up, the whistle blows.
explanation.incorrect: Delayed offside doesn't last forever. Once the attacking team plays the puck while someone is still offside, the linesman blows it dead.

lessons.title: Icing, and why teams hate it
lessons.objective: Describe what icing is and its penalty.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition of icing.
payload.template: Icing is shooting the puck from your own half across the opposing {{line}}, and it only counts if the puck is {{state}}.

explanation.correct: Right. It's a clear from your own half that slides all the way past the far goal line with nobody touching it. Teams do it to relieve pressure, and it costs them.
explanation.incorrect: Icing needs two things: the puck goes from your own half across the opposing goal line, and nobody touches it on the way.

payload.prompt: Icing gives the other team a power play. True or false?

scene.alt: A puck sliding down the ice and being called icing.

explanation.correct: False. Icing is not a penalty. No power play. The cost is: faceoff in your zone and you cannot change players.
explanation.incorrect: Icing is a stoppage, not a penalty. No power play, just a bad restart position.

payload.prompt: Match what happens after icing is called.

pairs.definition: The faceoff happens in the zone of the team that iced it.
The team that iced cannot swap players; they must defend with the same line.
The same players stay on the ice, creating fatigue and pressure in your own end.

explanation.summary: Icing isn't a penalty, but it stings: a faceoff in your own end and no fresh legs to defend it.
explanation.sayThisLine: They iced it, so they can't change.

payload.prompt: Your team leads late and ices the puck. What's the biggest problem?

options.text: The other team gets a power play
You defend a faceoff in your own zone with tired skaters who can't change
You automatically lose your lead

explanation.correct: Right. The clear bought a moment, but the same tired skaters must defend a faceoff in their own end. That's why teams try hard not to ice it at the end of a shift.
explanation.incorrect: Icing is a stoppage, not a penalty, so there's no power play and no change to the score. The cost is a defensive-zone faceoff with the same tired skaters.

payload.prompt: A clear from your half bounces off the side boards, then crosses the far goal line untouched. Icing?

scene.alt: A puck shot from the defensive half bounces off the side boards and slides across the far goal line.

explanation.correct: Icing. The boards don't count as a touch. What matters is that it left your half and crossed the far goal line with nobody playing it.
explanation.incorrect: A bounce off the boards isn't a touch by a player. Untouched from your half to the far goal line is still icing.

lessons.title: Be the linesman: hybrid icing
lessons.objective: Decide when hybrid icing is called.

payload.prompt: How does the linesman call hybrid icing?

options.text: When a player first touches the puck
When the linesman sees the other team's skater would win the race to the faceoff dots
When the puck reaches the goal line, whoever is closer

explanation.correct: Right. The linesman watches the race to the end-zone faceoff dots. If the retriever from the other team is ahead, he whistles it before anyone touches the puck.
explanation.incorrect: The linesman judges the race to the end-zone faceoff dots: if the skater from the team that didn't ice would get there first, it's icing. Nobody has to touch the puck.

payload.prompt: Hybrid icing was introduced to prevent high-speed collisions at the boards. True or false?

scene.alt: Two players racing toward the boards at high speed.

explanation.correct: True. Racing into the boards caused serious injuries, so the NHL adopted hybrid icing, where the race is judged at the faceoff dots and ends there.
explanation.incorrect: It was a safety move. Hybrid icing lets the linesman decide at the faceoff dots, so skaters don't have to race all the way into the boards.

payload.prompt: Match the icing style to how it worked.

pairs.definition: Older rule: icing only counts once a player touches the puck, so skaters raced into the boards.
Current NHL rule: the linesman judges the race at the faceoff dots and whistles it before a touch.
Whistled the moment the puck crosses the goal line; used in many youth leagues.

explanation.summary: Hybrid icing sits between the old race to the boards and automatic icing, and it keeps skaters safer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hybrid means the race ends at the dots.

payload.prompt: The team that iced has a skater clearly ahead in the race to the dots. What happens?

options.text: Icing is called anyway
Icing is waved off and play continues
The referee asks the other linesman

explanation.correct: Right. If the chaser is ahead, the linesman waves it off and play goes on. Icing is called only when the other team's retriever would get there first.
explanation.incorrect: When the skater from the team that iced is ahead, there's no icing. It's called only when the retriever from the other team would win the race to the dots.

lessons.title: When icing does not apply
lessons.objective: Know why a shorthanded team can freely ice.

payload.prompt: A team on the penalty kill (down a player) can ice the puck without a stoppage. True or false?

scene.alt: A shorthanded team clears the puck from their defensive zone with 4 skaters on ice.

explanation.correct: True. A team shorthanded because of a penalty can't be called for icing, so it can fire the puck down the ice to burn time and get a breather.
explanation.incorrect: A team killing a penalty can't be called for icing. The rule gives it a way to relieve pressure while it's a skater down.

payload.prompt: Can a team on the power play (the attacking team) ice without it being called?

options.text: Yes, same as the penalty-kill team
No, icing is called against them like any other team
Only if their power play is failing

explanation.correct: Right. The team with the extra skater plays under the normal icing rule. Only the shorthanded team is exempt.
explanation.incorrect: Only the shorthanded team can ice freely. The power-play team is held to the normal icing rule, so it faces the same defensive-zone faceoff and no-change penalty as anyone.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to why icing exemption exists.

pairs.definition: Down a player because a teammate is in the penalty box.
The benefit of the exemption: clear the puck down the ice and get a breather while a skater down.
The goal is to survive the penalty, and a legal, free clear helps burn time.

explanation.summary: The exemption is a bit of fairness: a team a skater down gets to clear the puck without being punished for it.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're shorthanded, so they can ice it for free.

payload.prompt: If the puck is deflected before reaching the goal line, it is not icing. True or false?

scene.alt: A puck is touched (deflected) by a player's stick before crossing the goal line.

explanation.correct: True. If any player touches the puck on its way, it's no longer an untouched clear, so there's no icing.
explanation.incorrect: A deflection means somebody touched the puck. Icing needs a clear that is untouched from the defensive half to the goal line.

payload.prompt: A clear from deep in your own end slides into the opposing net. What's the call?

options.text: Icing, because it crossed the goal line untouched
A goal for your team
No goal, and a faceoff

explanation.correct: Right. A puck that goes into the net is a goal, and a goal beats icing. This is how a lot of empty-net goals happen.
explanation.incorrect: Icing doesn't apply when the puck goes into the net. It's a goal, and that's how most empty-net goals are scored.

lessons.title: Goal, no goal: review and challenges
lessons.objective: Explain what coaches can challenge and what it costs.

payload.prompt: What can an NHL coach challenge?

options.text: Any call he disagrees with
A goal that followed an offside entry or goalie interference
Only penalties

explanation.correct: Right. Challenges are limited to specific things, mainly a goal after an offside entry or goalie interference, plus a missed stoppage. The league also reviews every goal itself.
explanation.incorrect: Challenges are narrow. A coach can't contest any call; he can ask for a video look at a goal that came after an offside entry, goalie interference or a missed stoppage.

payload.prompt: A coach can challenge as often as he likes, risk-free. True or false?

scene.alt: A coach signals for a video review and the review upholds the call on the ice.

explanation.correct: False. A failed challenge costs the team something (a timeout or a penalty, depending on the rules of the season), so coaches only challenge when they're fairly sure.
explanation.incorrect: It isn't free. A failed challenge carries a cost, so coaches pick their spots. The exact price has changed over the years, so check the current rulebook.

payload.prompt: A challenge for goalie interference succeeds. What happens to the goal?

options.text: It stands, but the coach is fined
It comes off the board and play restarts with a faceoff
The other team gets a power play

explanation.correct: Right. A successful challenge wipes out the goal, and there's no penalty on the attacking team. Play restarts with a faceoff and the challenge counts as a win.
explanation.incorrect: When the review agrees with the coach, the goal is cancelled and the game restarts with a faceoff. There's no power play or fine.

payload.prompt: Match the review term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The coach asks for a video review of a goal for one of a few specific reasons.
The review agrees with the coach and the on-ice call is reversed.
The review upholds the on-ice call, and the challenging team pays a price.

explanation.summary: Challenging is a gamble: win and the call is reversed, lose and it costs you, so coaches are selective.
explanation.sayThisLine: The challenge worked, it was offside.

payload.prompt: A goal against might be offside. Do you challenge?

situation.narrative: Third period, tied 2-2. The other team just scored. Your video coach says the entry looked close.

facts.label: Cost of a failed challenge
facts.value: A real penalty for your team

options.label: Challenge, but only because the replay shows a clear skate over
options.consequence: If the review agrees, the goal is wiped out and the score is tied again.
considerations: Confidence matters more than the score.
A clear skate over the line is the kind of call that gets overturned.

options.label: Challenge anyway; you're down and have nothing to lose
options.consequence: A failed challenge can cost you a penalty and hand over a power play while you trail by a goal.
considerations: Failed challenges have a price, and it hurts most in a tight third period.
A coin-flip challenge is how teams give away special-teams time.

options.label: Let it go and focus on the next shift
options.consequence: You avoid the risk, but you may be giving up a goal that wasn't legal.
considerations: If the video coach isn't sure, skipping is reasonable.
Weigh how clear the replay is against the cost of being wrong.

payload.expertNote: Coaches challenge when the video staff is confident, because the cost of a failed challenge is real. Hearing 'they challenged and lost' tells you the review saw it differently from the bench.
payload.sayThisLine: They were sure enough to challenge, and they were right.

lessons.title: The crease and goalie contact
lessons.objective: Explain why some goals get waved off.

payload.prompt: Light incidental contact between an attacker and the goalie always cancels the goal. True or false?

scene.alt: Slight contact between an attacker and a goalie in the crease.

explanation.correct: False. Light contact is okay. Only contact that impairs the save is interference.
explanation.incorrect: Goalie interference requires the contact to actually prevent the save. Light touch alone is not enough.

payload.prompt: Complete the interference rule.
payload.template: A goal is waved off when an attacker's contact or position {{effect}} the goalie's ability to make a {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Interference is about effect: did the attacker's contact or position keep the goalie from making the save? If yes, no goal.
explanation.incorrect: What counts is the effect. Standing in the crease isn't enough; the attacker's contact or position has to impair the goalie's chance to make a save.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to its role in crease contact.

pairs.definition: The blue painted area in front of the goal; attackers can enter but cannot impair the goalie.
Touching the goalie is okay if it does not affect their ability to move or save.
Prevent the goalie from being in position or from moving to make a save.

explanation.summary: The crease is shared space; interference is about the effect of the contact, not just being there.
explanation.sayThisLine: He didn't touch the goalie, so it should count.

payload.prompt: Attacker pushes goalie away and puck goes in. It is a goal. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker pushing a goalie away from the post as the puck slides in.

explanation.correct: False. The attacker moved the goalie out of position, so the goal is waved off for interference.
explanation.incorrect: If the attacker's own action keeps the goalie from making the save, the goal doesn't count. (If a defender had shoved the attacker into the goalie, it would be different.)

payload.prompt: Is it legal to stand in the crease and screen the goalie?

options.text: No, any attacker in the crease blocks the goal
Yes, if you do not push or move the goalie
Only if the puck is in the air

explanation.correct: Right. Screening (standing in front) is legal. Interference is about contact that prevents the save.
explanation.incorrect: Attackers can legally stand in the crease and screen. It is only interference if they impair the goalie's movement.
